Overview

Accra as a Business Centre

Accra is Ghana's capital and its main business centre. The Greater Accra Region recorded 5,455,692 residents at the 2021 Population and Housing Census, 17.7 percent of the national total, and overtook Ashanti as the most populous region. The city hosts the presidency, ministries, the central bank, the main regulators and the headquarters of most Ghanaian banks, insurers and law firms, as well as the West African offices of many multinational companies. The neighbouring port city of Tema, linked to Accra by road and rail, handles much of the country's container trade, and the international airport in Accra connects Ghana with the rest of Africa, Europe and the Middle East.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Accra because decisions about Ghana's mining, cocoa, oil and gas, energy, telecoms and infrastructure sectors are taken there, and because government contracts, licences and permits are negotiated with ministries and agencies in the capital. Typical engagements include diligence on local partners and politically connected shareholders, review of agents and intermediaries in public procurement, verification of gold and commodity suppliers, and tracing of assets after a contract dispute or arbitration. Accra is also where most Ghanaian commercial litigation is heard, so litigation history, witnesses and enforcement prospects usually lead back to the city.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Accra

01

Local partner and shareholder diligence

Investors entering Ghana often take Accra-based partners for licensing, local content or market access reasons. Diligence identifies the partner's real owners, political exposure, prior disputes, tax and regulatory issues, and whether relationships with officials could create bribery or conflict-of-interest risk.

02

Public procurement and intermediaries

Government contracts in energy, roads, health and digital services are awarded through ministries and agencies in Accra. Reviews of agents, consultants and subcontractors examine ownership, links to officials, capacity to perform and history in prior tenders, supporting anti-bribery compliance and contract decisions.

03

Gold and commodity supplier verification

Buyers and refiners sourcing gold, cocoa or other commodities through Accra-registered exporters verify licences, ownership, source of supply and links to informal or illegal mining. Research combines registry data, regulator announcements, court records and Ghanaian press to assess provenance and reputational exposure.

04

Asset tracing after disputes

Creditors holding judgments or arbitral awards against Ghanaian parties need to locate real estate, company interests and receivables, much of it in Accra. Work maps corporate holdings and property, identifies transfers to relatives or affiliates, and supports counsel in planning enforcement.

05

Banking and fintech counterparty reviews

Accra hosts Ghana's banks, mobile money operators and a growing fintech sector. Partners, acquirers and correspondent banks review licensing status, ownership changes, regulatory sanctions and fraud or insolvency history before entering relationships with Accra financial institutions.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Accra

High Court Commercial Division

Ghana has a specialised commercial division of the High Court for high-value business disputes involving contracts, banking, insurance and import and export transactions, and its principal sittings are in Accra. Its rules provide for short pleading timelines, a pre-trial settlement conference and a settlement period of up to 60 days before trial, though delays are common. Appeals go to the Court of Appeal as of right and then to the Supreme Court, both of which sit in Accra.

Arbitration and ADR in Accra

Arbitration and mediation are governed by the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act, 2010 (Act 798), which is broadly based on the UNCITRAL Model Law, requires courts to stay proceedings in favour of valid arbitration agreements and limits challenges to awards. The Ghana Arbitration Centre and the Ghana ADR Hub are described as the country's two foremost arbitral institutions, and court-connected ADR has settled more than 37,000 cases over two decades.

Registries and investment agencies

Company registration is handled by the Office of the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 2019, which replaced the 1963 Act; national ownership disclosure rules are covered on our Ghana page. Enterprises with foreign participation must also register with the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre, and export-oriented businesses can operate under the free zones regime established in 1995. These bodies are headquartered in Accra, making their public records an early stop in any review.

Regulators and national institutions

As the capital, Accra hosts the central bank, the securities and insurance regulators, the stock exchange and the anti-corruption and audit institutions. Their published decisions, sanctions lists, licensing registers and reports are key lawful sources on Ghanaian banks, listed companies and public bodies, and Accra-based newspapers such as the Daily Graphic provide the most consistent reporting on business disputes and enforcement.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Accra

For Accra matters TDSC first identifies which parties are registered or operate in the capital, which sit in Tema, Kumasi or the mining regions, and which are held offshore. Research draws on Registrar of Companies information available through lawful channels, regulator and agency publications, Ghanaian court decisions and Accra press, reviewed by researchers familiar with Ghanaian business and politics. Where interviews, site visits or retrieval of court and land documents are needed, TDSC coordinates qualified Ghanaian professionals and works under the direction of the client's Ghanaian counsel, respecting Ghana's data protection law. Politically exposed persons and public procurement links receive particular attention, and every counterparty is screened for sanctions exposure.

TDSC has no office in Accra. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Accra: Frequently Asked Questions

Why do most Ghana matters lead to Accra?

Accra is the seat of government, the central bank, the main regulators and most Ghanaian banks and law firms, and the Greater Accra Region is the country's most populous. Even where a mine, farm or plant is elsewhere, contracts, licences, ownership decisions and litigation usually run through the capital.

Where are commercial disputes heard in Accra?

High-value business disputes go to the commercial division of the High Court, which applies rules designed to encourage early settlement, including a pre-trial settlement conference. Appeals go to the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court. Many contracts instead provide for arbitration under the ADR Act, 2010 (Act 798).

Which arbitration institutions operate in Accra?

The Ghana Arbitration Centre and the Ghana ADR Hub are regarded as the country's leading arbitral institutions. The ADR Act, 2010 governs arbitration and mediation, requires courts to refer disputes to arbitration where there is a valid agreement, and limits court interference with awards. Court-connected mediation is also widely used.

Can TDSC check whether an Accra partner is politically exposed?

Yes, within lawful limits. Research uses company records, public appointment and procurement information, court decisions and Ghanaian press to identify links between a partner and public officials or political figures. Findings are presented with their sources, distinguishing documented relationships from reputation or rumour, so counsel can assess bribery and conflict risk.

Does TDSC have an office in Accra?

No. TDSC is based in Nashville, Tennessee and has no office or staff in Ghana. Engagements touching Accra are scoped and managed from Nashville. Where local work is required, TDSC coordinates qualified Ghanaian professionals and works with the client's Ghanaian counsel, and it does not claim any Ghanaian licence.
